whatIs.title: What Is WebP, and Why Convert From PNG?
whatIs.content: WebP is a modern image format developed by Google in 2010, combining the best capabilities of JPG, PNG, and GIF into a single format. It uses a prediction-based compression algorithm derived from VP8 video encoding for lossy mode, and DEFLATE-like LZ77 with Huffman coding for lossless mode. Unlike JPG (lossy-only) or PNG (lossless-only), WebP supports both compression modes plus full alpha channel transparency — making it a genuine superset that can replace both formats depending on your quality requirements.
whatIs.content2: Real-world size results are dramatic: a 2 MB PNG hero banner typically becomes 300–500 KB in lossy WebP at quality 80 (75–85% reduction), or 1.2–1.6 MB in lossless WebP (20–40% reduction). Both modes preserve full alpha transparency if present in the source PNG. For photographic content where minor imperceptible compression is acceptable, lossy WebP at quality 80–85 is virtually indistinguishable from the PNG source at any typical viewport size.
whatIs.content3: Browser support is universal among evergreen browsers — Chrome 23+, Edge 18+, Firefox 65+, Opera 12.1+, and Safari 14+ all decode WebP natively, covering well over 97% of global browser usage as of 2025. For the rare legacy holdouts (IE 11, very old Safari), use a picture element with WebP as the primary source and PNG as the fallback — the browser picks whichever format it understands.

whyWebp.title: Why Use WebP for Web Images?
whyWebp.content: Google's Core Web Vitals measure page load experience using three metrics, of which **Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)** is heavily influenced by image size. Replacing a 2 MB PNG hero image with a 400 KB WebP at the same perceived quality can move your LCP from 'poor' (over 4 s on mobile) to 'good' (under 2.5 s) without a single code change beyond the image src. For sites with multiple large images above the fold, this effect compounds significantly. whyWebp.content2: WebP also reduces CDN egress costs and per-pageview bandwidth consumption — relevant for any site paying for data transfer. On mobile networks where users are on data caps (particularly in Asia, Latin America, and Africa), faster and lighter images translate directly to reduced bounce rates and higher engagement. E-commerce conversion research consistently shows that faster product image loads correlate with higher add-to-cart rates. For SaaS dashboards, marketing pages, and content-heavy sites, the upgrade from PNG to WebP is one of the highest-ROI performance improvements available.

whyWebp.content2: WebP also reduces bandwidth for your CDN, speeds up mobile page loads on slow networks, and saves data for users on capped plans. For e-commerce and content-heavy sites, the upgrade is nearly always worth it.

step2.title: 2. Choose Lossy or Lossless
step2.content: Leave Lossless off for photos — lossy WebP at quality 80–85 delivers the best balance of file size and visual fidelity. Enable Lossless only for graphics or synthetic images (logos, diagrams) where artifacts on flat colors or sharp edges are unacceptable. For JPG sources, lossless WebP makes little sense: the JPG is already lossy, so lossless re-encoding merely preserves existing artifacts in a larger file.

step3.title: 3. Pick a Quality (Lossy Only)
step3.content: The default quality of 80 hits the sweet spot for most photographic content — minimal visible difference at a 25–35% file size reduction. Quality 75–85 is appropriate for hero images, thumbnails, and product photos. Drop to 70–75 only for low-importance background images where some softening is acceptable.

At quality 80, most photographic content is imperceptibly different from the source while occupying 30% less disk and CDN bandwidth.

photo.title: Photo-Optimized
photo.content: WebP's lossy codec (VP8) uses adaptive block quantization and entropy coding tailored to continuous-tone images. It handles gradients, skin tones, and low-contrast areas cleanly — areas where JPEG introduces noticeable banding or blocking artifacts at comparable file sizes. This makes WebP especially effective for photography when you need to trim bytes without touching perceived quality.

whatIs.title: What is EXIF metadata and why remove it?
whatIs.content: EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) is hidden data silently embedded in almost every photo your phone or camera takes. It records the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was captured, the device make and model, camera settings, timestamps down to the second, and even which software last edited the file. This metadata is invisible when you view the image but travels with the file wherever it goes — attached to every upload, every email, every message you share.
whatIs.content2: For most people, the GPS coordinates are the alarming part. A single vacation photo posted online can pinpoint your home address if it was taken in your backyard. A product photo on a marketplace reveals where you live. A portrait shared with a stranger discloses the room you were in. Device identifiers additionally fingerprint you across multiple uploads, letting anyone correlate anonymous posts back to the same camera.
whatIs.content3: This tool strips every EXIF tag from your photo while keeping the image visually identical. For HEIC files it performs a binary-level metadata removal with zero re-encoding, so the original compression quality is perfectly preserved. For other formats it re-encodes through a pipeline that extracts the ICC colour profile before cleaning and re-embeds it afterwards, so your colours never shift.

whyRemove.title: What privacy risks does photo metadata expose?
whyRemove.content: GPS coordinates are precise to roughly 10 metres — enough to identify the exact house, the specific room in an office building, or the table at a restaurant. Combined with a timestamp accurate to the second, a single photo reveals where you were, when you were there, and for many modern phones, which direction you were facing. Threat actors have used this data to stalk individuals, map daily routines, and identify safe houses from photos posted by well-meaning supporters.
whyRemove.content2: Device metadata is a subtler but persistent tracker. The combination of camera make, model, and serial number creates a hardware fingerprint that stays identical across every photo from that device. Platforms and data brokers use this fingerprint to correlate accounts: the anonymous photo you posted to one forum and the product photo on your marketplace listing can be linked to the same device even if you used different names. Software tags additionally leak your editing workflow — which version of Photoshop, Lightroom, or mobile app touched the file — painting a detailed picture of your tooling to anyone paying attention.

All other formats go through an ICC-profile-aware re-encoding pipeline: the embedded colour profile is extracted before cleaning and re-embedded afterwards, so your greens stay green and your skies stay blue.

useCases.title: When you should strip EXIF before sharing

social.title: Social Media Sharing
social.content: Before posting photos to social platforms, especially ones that expose downloadable originals like Flickr, Imgur, or direct-link image hosts. Even platforms that claim to strip metadata on upload sometimes leak GPS through other channels — stripping it client-side first guarantees nothing sensitive leaves your device.

marketplace.title: Online Marketplace Listings
marketplace.content: When listing items on marketplaces like eBay, Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, or Mercari. Product photos taken at home embed your GPS coordinates directly into the listing photo, giving every potential buyer a precise route to your front door. Strip it before uploading and protect your home address.

album.title: Shared Photo Albums
album.content: Before sharing vacation photo albums via cloud links (Dropbox, Google Drive, iCloud Photos) with anyone outside your immediate family. Shared links often propagate unpredictably, and each photo in the album carries independent GPS data — a shared link to 50 holiday photos maps out exactly where you stayed every night of the trip.

journalism.title: Journalism & Sensitive Sources
journalism.content: For journalists, researchers, and leakers handling sensitive source material. Photos of documents, locations, or informants carry embedded evidence of where and when they were captured, which device took them, and which editing software processed them. Stripping this metadata is a non-negotiable step in any operational security workflow.

whatIsMetadata.a: Photo metadata — collectively known as EXIF, IPTC, and XMP tags — is structured data embedded inside the image file itself, separate from the visible pixel data. It includes GPS latitude/longitude, capture timestamp, camera make and model, lens information, ISO/shutter/aperture settings, editing history, software versions, and sometimes even thumbnail previews or drone flight paths. All of this travels silently attached to the file whenever you share it.

heicQuality.q: Will cleaning HEIC reduce the image quality?
heicQuality.a: No — HEIC cleaning is fully lossless in this tool. We use ExifTool to strip metadata at the binary level without touching the compressed pixel data, which means the output is bit-for-bit identical to the original in every area except the metadata boxes. This is different from most competitors that re-encode HEIC through a lossy HEIC encoder and introduce subtle quality loss. Verify it yourself: the cleaned file will be the same dimensions and nearly identical file size to the original.

colorShift.q: Will my colours look different after cleaning?
colorShift.a: No — ICC colour profiles are preserved. For JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, and TIFF, we extract the embedded ICC profile (for example sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB) before removing metadata and re-embed it into the cleaned file. This means photos edited in wide-gamut workspaces and exported with Display P3 will continue to render accurately on compatible displays. HEIC files keep their original profile automatically since no re-encoding happens.
